$schema-note: The mutant list, per unit, as data -- which is what closes Risk R13.
Every slice in the plan reports a mutation tally and none of them could be re-run: the mutants
were hand edits in a scratch worktree and were thrown away, so a tally was an assertion rather
than a measurement (Risk R13, plan section 6.145). A mutant here is a find/replace against one
ported file plus what it is EXPECTED to do, and `python tools/mutate.py` turns the tally back
into a command.
FIELDS.
unit.name     what to pass to --unit
unit.slice    the plan row this list belongs to
unit.filter   substrings handed to the test runner, one per TEST_CLASS that covers this
unit, so a mutant runs its own tests rather than all 349
unit.tests    how many tests those filters select, VERIFIED against the unmutated build
before any mutant is applied. A filter that selects the wrong tests reports
survivors for code it never ran, which is worse than no filter at all --
`hyperspace` was recorded as "Hyperspace" and matched three tests in other
files whose method names contain the word (plan section 6.147)
mutant.id     the name the plan uses for it, where the plan named one
mutant.find   text that must appear EXACTLY ONCE in the file; the run fails loudly if not,
because a mutant that silently applied nowhere is a mutant reported as caught
mutant.expect caught | survives | equivalent | uncompilable
mutant.selftest  true on the one mutant per unit whose job is to prove the HARNESS works --
an unmissable change the suite cannot fail to catch. A run in which a selftest
mutant survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless, and the tool
stops there rather than reporting a tally (Risk R13, plan section 6.119)
`expect: caught` is the normal case and anything else must say why in its note. A run fails
when an outcome differs from its expectation in EITHER direction: a new survivor is a gap in
the tests, and a recorded survivor that starts being caught is debt that has been paid and
should be written down as paid.

units.name: tactics
note: The ship AI and the autopilot (plan section 6.125). The docking half is closed -- every
`dock-*` and `steer-*` mutation is caught after sections 6.131 and 6.132 found three
branches its sweep could not reach. The AI half is not: fifteen survivors are recorded in
the plan BY NAME and are the reason this file exists.
HOW THE FIFTEEN GOT HERE, stated plainly because it bears on what a first run means. The
original mutants were hand edits and are gone; what survives is their names in section
6.125. Each name points at a constant or an operation that appears exactly once in
`Tactics.cpp` -- `ta-253` at the `CMP #253`, `msl-bit5` at the `BIT M32+1`, and so on -- so
the edit below is reconstructed from the name and from the routine, not recovered.
That makes the first run of this unit a TEST OF THE RECONSTRUCTION as much as of the port:
a reconstructed mutant that survives confirms the name was read correctly, and one that is
caught means either the reconstruction missed or the debt is smaller than recorded. Either
answer is worth more than the fifteen names were, because from here on the mutant is the
data and the name is just its label.
THE FIRST RUN, 2026-09-05, on the MSVC leg with a green 348-test baseline: 16 mutants, 3
caught, 13 survived. The three caught are the selftest, `ta7-three` and `msl-kill`; the
other thirteen survive exactly as section 6.125 recorded. So the measured debt is THIRTEEN
and not fifteen -- and the two that came back caught are the honest limit of this exercise,
because the original mutants are gone and nothing can say whether the reconstruction missed
or the debt was overstated. Thirteen re-runnable survivors is still thirteen more than the
corpus had yesterday.
The method for closing them is section 6.132's and is unchanged: probe the comparison,
count the distinct values that reach it, and add a ladder to the fixture. All fifteen are
thresholds the geometry table never lands on.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Dropping one of TAS6's three EOR #%10000000s leaves the negated vector wrong on the y axis, and TheNegationMatchesTAS6 compares all three against the shipped routine. Its job is to prove this run OBSERVES a catch -- without it, fifteen 'survivors' below could all be a harness that never rebuilt. Keep it first and never delete it.
The station's launch roll, three times in 256. The sweep's seeds never land on 252.
TN5's police roll. Same shape as ta-253: a threshold with no case beside it.
The Anaconda's escort roll, CMP #200 at TN7's entrance -- not the hermit's CMP #200.
TN7's six-times-in-256 roll that gives a ship a random pitch.
ORA #104 on the roll TN7 just made. Only reachable through ta-250's branch.
How often a badly damaged ship with a pod actually runs.
TA7's LSR A -- energy above HALF the blueprint maximum and the ship fights on.

The second energy test, below which a ship may run, nested inside ta-half's. CAUGHT on the first run, by TheAiMatchesTACTICS, while the plan names `ta7-three` among fifteen survivors. Since the original mutant is gone, this says one of two things and does not say which: the reconstruction is not the edit that was made, or that item of debt does not exist. What it does settle is that THIS perturbation of the shift is distinguished, and it stays here as a caught mutant rather than being deleted, because a mutant that is caught is still evidence.
LDA ECMA / BNE TA3 -- a running ECM stops the launch and the missile is not spent.

TA20's EOR #%10000000 on the MISSILE path in part 4. The identical two lines appear again on the `reverse` path below, so the mutant carries the NegateVector call above it to be unique -- and that is the second thing this pins: which of the two TA20 entrances is being measured.
TA64's CMP #16 -- one frame in sixteen a missile checks its target's ECM.
A missile that reaches slot 1 -- the station -- dies rather than exploding.
BIT M32+1 read as data: bit 5 is 'already exploding', so this is 'do not blow up a wreck'.

LDA #250 / JMP OOPS -- what a missile that has arrived costs, against the 80 a near miss costs. CAUGHT on the first run, by TheAiMatchesTACTICS, while the plan names `msl-kill` among fifteen survivors; the same caveat as ta7-three applies. 250 against 80 is a large difference in the player's energy banks and the sweep compares all three, so this one being caught is unsurprising -- which is itself a hint that the original `msl-kill` mutated something smaller.
TA87's AND #%01111111 / LSR A -- the AI byte becomes the TARGET's slot for EXNO2.

units.name: hyperspace
note: The jump, witchspace and the galactic hyperdrive (plan section 6.136). Seeded with three
mutants rather than a full sweep, and they are here to prove the HARNESS rather than the
slice: two constants that a green suite must notice, and one recorded equivalent so the
'expect' field is exercised in more than one state.
A full list for this unit is work the next slice to touch it should do, and that is the
shape this file is meant to grow in: a slice adds its own mutants when it lands, instead of
reporting a number nobody can check.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent. Inverting 'is this a space view' changes whether the hyperspace tunnel is drawn at all, so TheJumpMatchesTT18 cannot miss it. Its job is not to measure the port -- it is to prove that this harness still OBSERVES a catch, applies its edit to the file the build actually compiles, and rebuilds between mutants. Risk R13's realised form was a harness that reported catches it never saw (section 6.119); a run in which this one survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless. Keep it first in the list and never delete it.

CMP #253 / BCS MJP -- three jumps in 256 mis-jump, and `>=` to `>` makes it two. SURVIVED on this tool's first run, and it is a real gap rather than an equivalent. TheJumpMatchesTT18 sweeps four generator seeds by three fuels by three distances by four views, and its own comment says the seeds were chosen so that BOTH SIDES of the CMP are reached -- which they are. Reaching both sides is not landing ON the boundary, and 253 exactly is never rolled, so the one value that tells `>=` from `>` is the one value never tried. Section 6.132 in a new instance: the counter wanted is distinct answers per BRANCH, and here it is distinct values at the branch. Closing it is a seed that rolls 253.

JSR CTRL / AND PATG / BMI ptg -- the cheat needs BOTH the key and the option, and `&&` to `||` is not caught. Nothing in TheJump varies the two flags: TheCheatFlagMatchesPtg tests `ptg` ALONE, over all 256 values of COK, and never enters PerformJump. The `&&` was also unreachable in the app until 2026-09-05, because JumpOf hardcoded controlHeld to false (section 6.147) -- so the fix that made the galactic hyperdrive reachable also made this gap matter, and the tool found it the same day. Closing it is four cases in PerformJump over the two flags.

A deliberate no-op: 0 and 0u are the same std::uint8_t. It is here so a run exercises the equivalent path, and it must never be 'caught' -- if it is, the harness is reporting on something other than the edit it made.

units.name: trumbles
note: MVTRIBS and the six Trumble sprites (plan section 6.148). Ten mutants, written with the
slice rather than reconstructed from a name, so this unit is a measurement from its first
run rather than a test of a reconstruction.
The two that matter most are `tr-carry2` and `tr-carry1`. The routine takes two random
numbers with DIFFERENT carries -- the first clear because an `ASL A` on a value below eight
cannot carry, the second set because `CMP #235` set it on the way past -- and the generator
reads C. Neither shows on screen; both move the whole sequence.
FIRST RUN, 2026-09-05, on the portable leg with a green 355-test baseline: 11 mutants, 9
caught and 2 survived. Both survivors were answered rather than recorded as debt.
`tr-leftsign` was a GAP and is closed: restricted to the 0 and 1 that MVTRIBS writes back,
the high byte of the x calculation can only come out as 0, 1, 2 or &FF, and &FF has every
bit set -- so bit 6 answers exactly as bit 7 does. Nothing in the library initialises
TRIBXH, TRIBVX or TRIBVXH, so the first pass after a Trumble appears reads uninitialised
RAM, and `TheSignTestReadsBitSeven` is that pass: all 256 starting values, which is where
the two bits disagree.
`tr-msb-or` is a PROVABLE EQUIVALENT and is recorded as one. See its note.
REWRITTEN 2026-09-05 when main's sprite work landed. `SPMASK` is no longer ported --
`VideoState` gives each sprite a whole sixteen-bit x, so the pair of masks that clear and
set one sprite's bit in a shared register have nothing to mask -- and `tr-spritebit` and
`tr-msb-or` went with it. `tr-sprite-index` and `tr-ninth-bit` cover the store that
replaced them.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Dropping the y velocity leaves every Trumble on the row it started on, and TheYWrapMatchesMVTRIBS compares 768 rows against the shipped routine. Its job is to prove this run OBSERVES a catch; a run in which it survives is a run whose every other answer is worthless (Risk R13, plan section 6.119). Keep it first and never delete it.

The SECOND DORND's carry, which `CMP #235` set on the way past. Wrong here and the y velocity is drawn from a different entry of TRIBDIR about half the time AND the generator ends one state adrift, so the next frame's roll is wrong too. Nothing on screen would say so; TheDirectionChoiceMatchesMVTRIBS compares RAND.
The FIRST DORND's carry, which is the `ASL A` two instructions above -- clear, because A is at most 7. The mirror image of tr-carry2 and it fails on the same comparison.
`CMP TRIBCT / BCC` -- the pass on which the counter EQUALS the count must not move anything. Off by one and a hold with three Trumbles moves a fourth sprite that is not showing.
`AND #7` -- with three left it counts to three instead of seven, so a Trumble moves every fourth frame rather than every eighth and the sixth one never moves at all.
`CMP #235 / BCC MVTR1` -- the boundary itself. Told apart only by a seed that rolls exactly 235, and the direction sweep tries 256 seeds against six sprites.
`CMP #&50 / BCC oktrib` -- &150 exactly is off the right edge and &14F is not. The x sweep walks all 256 low bytes, so the boundary is in it by construction.

`BPL nominus` reads bit 7 and nothing else. SURVIVED on the first run, because within the 0 and 1 that MVTRIBS writes back to TRIBXH the high byte can only be 0, 1, 2 or &FF and &FF has bit 6 set as well. Closed by `TheSignTestReadsBitSeven`, which sweeps all 256 starting values of TRIBXH -- not an invented state, because nothing in the game initialises that byte and the first pass reads whatever the loader left.

`LDA #&48 / STA T` -- where a Trumble that walked off the left edge reappears. &48 rather than &50 is not arbitrary: at &150 the very next test would decide it had gone off the RIGHT edge and send it to zero, so this mutation makes the sprite teleport to the left edge instead of the right one.

The Trumbles are VIC-II sprites 2 to 7, not 0 to 5 -- sprites 0 and 1 are the laser sights and the explosion. Dropping the offset moves the wrong two sprites and leaves the top two Trumbles still, which the whole-register comparison sees on the first case.

The ninth x bit, dropped on the way into the register. This is the store that REPLACED `ORA SPMASK+1,Y / STA VIC+&10`: `VideoState` holds a whole sixteen-bit x, so the read-modify-write of a shared byte became one write, and this is the mutant that proves the second half of it is still there. A sprite past column 255 would sit on the left of the screen instead.

units.name: missions
note: The four control codes a mission briefing is made of (plan section 6.149).
TWO OF THESE ARE ABOUT A FALL-THROUGH. `PAUSE` ends `JSR LL9` and the next instruction is
MT23's `LDA #10`, so a briefing's `{22}` moves the cursor to row 10 and forces lower case as
surely as a `{23}` does. The port splits that across two objects -- the row is the seam's and
the two case flags are the text system's -- and the mutants below take one half away each.
FIRST RUN, 2026-09-05: 12 mutants, 9 caught, 3 survived, and all three were real gaps in the
sweep rather than debt. `mi-release` needed a keyboard that starts with a key DOWN;
`mi-mt9-view` needed a token that is not 216; `mi-pause2-loop` needed a scan count that does
not wrap -- and the mutant itself was replaced, because `if (x) continue;` at the top of a
`for(;;)` and `while (x) {}` are the same loop, so the first version could not have failed.

mutants.note: THE HARNESS'S OWN OracleIsPresent for this unit. Putting the briefing ship at z_hi = 0 rather than 2 draws it at a two-hundredth of the distance, which the whole-canvas comparison in TheBriefingShipMatchesPAS1 cannot miss. Keep it first and never delete it.

The byte the upstream comment gets wrong. `PAS1` on this build is `LDA #2 / STA INWK+7`; the Master and Apple versions load 1 and the comment was written for those. A port that trusted the comment would put the Constrictor at half the distance and twice the size, and this is the mutant that says so.
`conhieght`, which the source calls the size of a gap and which is really the ship's y coordinate. One row out is a whole-canvas difference.

The FIRST of PAUSE's two loops, dropped. `JSR PAS1 / BNE PAUSE` waits for the player to LET GO of the key that turned the previous page; without it one keystroke dismisses every remaining page of a briefing in a single frame. SURVIVED the first run, because the sweep always started with an empty keyboard and the loop is invisible from there -- closed by giving the script a `held` run, which is the state the loop exists for.
`LDA #0 / STA INWK+31` -- the ship stops being drawn, so the `LL9` after the screen change has nothing to rub out. Leaving the flags set makes that `LL9` erase lines the cleared screen no longer has.

The row PAUSE's fall-through moves to. MT23 loads 10 and MT29 loads 6, and the `EQUB &2C` between them is what makes the two one routine -- so this is the mutant that proves the port fell through into the right entry point.

PAUSE2's `BEQ PAUSE2` goes back to the TOP of the routine and not to the scan above it, so an empty second scan re-checks for a release the routine has already had. The mutant turns that into a do-while, which is the reading everybody has first. It shows only when the keyboard goes empty, empty, PRESSED: the real routine treats that third scan as 'still held' and goes round again, and the do-while takes it as the answer. Two scans apart, and nothing is drawn, so the scan count is the only instrument -- which is why the script counts calls in a byte that cannot wrap. The first version of this mutant was `continue` against an inner `while`, and those two ARE the same loop.

MT27 and MT28 swapped. The two ranges are three apart and OVERLAP, so galaxy 3's captain is galaxy 0's planet -- which means a swap is invisible for exactly one pair of inputs and visible for the rest. The sweep covers all eight galaxies of both.

`CLC / ADC GCNT` dropped, so every galaxy gets galaxy zero's captain. This is what the fixture itself did for an afternoon, by poking `GCNT` before `Mirror` overwrote it with the commander block -- `GCNT` is `TP+15`.
The token `BRIS` prints. 216 is INCOMING MESSAGE and 215 is a carriage return, so this is the mutant for a briefing that opens on a blank screen.
`LDY #100 / JMP DELAY` -- two seconds on PAL. Compared as a number rather than as elapsed time, because neither side has a raster.

MT9's column store, which the port did not have until this slice. `LDA #1 / JSR DOXC / JMP TT66` is one load serving two purposes, because `STA` does not touch the accumulator. SURVIVED the first run: the only token that reaches code 9 is 216, and it follows the `{9}` with an `{8}`, which moves the cursor to column 6 and hides the difference. Closed by `TheNewViewMatchesMT9`, which runs the code itself from a cursor at column 29.

mutants.find:
progress = static_cast<std::uint8_t>(progress | MISSION_1_STARTED);

    ShowIncomingMessage(_mission); // 6502: JSR BRIS
mutants.note: `LSR TP / SEC / ROL TP` sets bit 0; clearing it instead means the Constrictor is offered for ever. The sweep starts from sixteen values of TP so the flag is compared from states where it was already set as well as from states where it was not.

`BRIEF3`'s `AND #%11110000`, dropped. Picking the plans up also FORGETS mission 1 -- both its bits go -- and a port that only ORed would agree from every starting state whose low nibble was already zero, which is why the sweep walks sixteen of them.

`LSR TP / ASL TP` clears bit 0 and LEAVES BIT 1, which is what takes the pair from `%11` to `%10` -- finished and paid, and never offered again. Clearing both would leave it at `%00`, which reads as never started.

5,000 CREDITS IS 50,000 TENTHS. The cash is held in tenths of a credit throughout, so a reward written in credits pays a tenth of what the game pays -- and the whole commander block is compared, so it is the four cash bytes that say so.
`LDA #2 / STA ENGY` -- the navy's energy unit, which the flight loop reads as three units a pass where the shop's one gives two. A 1 is the shop's.
`INC TALLY+1` -- the HIGH byte, so the reward is 256 kills and a whole combat rank rather than one kill. This pair is low byte first, unlike the cash above it, which is exactly the trap.

Bit 4 set AFTER the question rather than before it. In the game the order matters -- `BCC BAYSTEP` leaves before the `INC` -- but the flag is set above the `DETOK` and nothing between the two reads it, so moving it past a print that cannot fail is the same program. Recorded as an equivalent so a run exercises that path, and it must never come back caught.
`INC TRIBBLE` -- the player leaves with ONE Trumble and `MLOOP`'s breeding does the rest. Two would double every population the game ever reaches.
`LDA #64 / STA MCNT` -- how long the Constrictor turns before it starts to move away. One frame out is a different screen and a different `MCNT` at the end, and both are compared.

The SECOND `INC INWK+6 / BEQ BR2` of the pair. The ship recedes two units a frame and the loop can end on either half, so dropping one halves the speed and changes which frame the briefing appears on.

`CPX #conhieght / BCC P%+4 / LDX #conhieght` clamps at the value rather than above it, and `>=` against `>` is the same clamp: the only value they treat differently is `conhieght` itself, which both leave at `conhieght`. An equivalent by construction, kept so the run exercises one.

`DEC MCNT` in the SECOND loop, which nothing branches on. The counter is live in the first loop and dead in the second, and dropping it there is invisible on screen -- so `MCNT` is compared as state, which is the only place it shows.
`.BR2 INC INWK+7` -- the high byte following the low one past 255. Without it the ship is 256 units nearer than the briefing text was written for, and `INWK` is compared byte for byte.
